intuition.summary: Tor measures the failure of tensoring to be exact: tensoring a monomorphism such as multiplication by 2 on Z with Z/2 kills it, and Tor records what is lost (the kernel).
intuition.source: G. Quick, MA3403 Algebraic Topology, Lecture 17 (NTNU 2018)

intuition.summary: Ext measures how far Hom(-,M) is from exact; e.g. 2: Z→Z induces a non-surjective map on Hom(-,Z/2), and Ext(A,M) is the cokernel that repairs this.
Tor_1(R/x, M) is the x-torsion of M for a non-zero-divisor x, which is the source of the name; over Z, Tor_1(Z/n,A) is the n-torsion of A and Tor(Q/Z,B) is the torsion subgroup of B.
Ext^1(A,B) as 'ways of gluing': classes of short exact sequences with sub B and quotient A, zero = split; higher Ext^n as n-step exact sequences (Yoneda).

A resolution spreads the information of a module over many degrees without changing homology; Ext^n is what H^n(Hom(-,Z)) sees, independent of the resolution. Another answer: via Dold-Kan, Hom into an injective resolution is a space whose homotopy groups are the Ext groups.
intuition.source: r/math Simple Questions thread (May 2020), answers by DamnShadowbans and Othenor

intuition.summary: Geometric picture: Tor computes derived intersections. Serre's formula takes the alternating sum of lengths of Tor_i(A/I,A/J) as intersection multiplicity; higher Tor vanish in the good (e.g. regular-sequence) case, and the naive length of A/I⊗A/J is only the Tor_0 term.
Ext^n(X,A) = Hom in the derived category from X to the shifted object A[n] (A[n] thought of as the n-fold delooping B^nA): Ext is 'maps up to homotopy into a shifted object'.

motivation.summary: Baer introduced Ext for abelian groups (1934) to classify extensions; Eilenberg-MacLane named it (1942) and used it in the universal coefficient theorem for cohomology; Cartan-Eilenberg (1956) defined it for modules over any ring.

Čech introduced Tor for abelian groups (1935); the name was coined by Eilenberg c.1950; first applications were Künneth and universal coefficient theorems in topology; Cartan-Eilenberg generalised to modules.
Topological motivation: homology with coefficients H_n(X;M) is homology of S_*(X)⊗M; since ⊗M is not left exact one needs Tor to relate H_n(X;M) to H_n(X)⊗M (universal coefficient theorem).
Cartan and Eilenberg developed derived functors to unify several separate cohomology theories (group, Lie algebra, associative algebra cohomology) as Ext/Tor over suitable rings.
motivation.source: D. Arapura, Ch.5 Derived functors and Tor

motivation.summary: lim^1 entered topology through Milnor's 1960 lim^1 sequence; Weibel treats R^n lim as a model derived functor beside Ext and Tor, with Mittag-Leffler giving vanishing.
Modern research motivation: vanishing of Ext/Tor detects freeness/projectivity (Auslander-Reiten conjecture: Ext^i(M,M⊕R)=0 for i>0 should force M free).

definitions.summary: Ext^n_R(A,B) as right derived functors of Hom(A,-) via an injective resolution of B, or of Hom(-,B) via a projective resolution of A; Cartan-Eilenberg showed both agree and are independent of the resolution.

Balance: Weibel §2.7 'Balancing Tor and Ext' proves the two derivations agree via a double complex whose rows/columns are exact; nLab likewise says the 'balanced Ext/Tor' are computed from a double complex and compared by two spectral sequences.
Symmetry of Tor proved with double complexes: if all rows and columns of a double complex are acyclic, the total complex homology matches both augmentations; apply to P⊗Q.
Over Z (a PID) a two-term free resolution 0→F1→F0→A→0 suffices: Ext(A,M)=coker(Hom(F0,M)→Hom(F1,M)), Tor(A,M)=ker(F1⊗M→F0⊗M); independence of the resolution via lifting lemma and chain homotopy.

Yoneda definition: degree i extensions 0→A→Z_{i-1}→...→Z_0→B→0 give classes in Ext^i(B,A); every class arises and equivalence of extensions matches equality of classes. This works in any abelian category without enough projectives.
Derived-category definition Ext^i(X,Y)=Hom_{D(A)}(X,Y[i]) for complexes; for objects A,B use A[0],B[0]. Stacks Lemma 13.27.6 identifies Ext^1 with the Homology-chapter Ext of extensions (§12.6).

Ext^1(A,B) ≅ equivalence classes of extensions of A by B (Weibel Thm 3.4.3), with Ext^1 as the obstruction to splitting (Lemma 3.4.1); group law via Baer sum (Def 3.4.4), built from pullback and pushout; Yoneda Ext^n as Vista 3.4.6.
Derived functors characterised as universal δ-functors; Ext^i identified with R^i Hom(M,-) by effaceability arguments.
Flatness via Tor: M flat iff Tor_1(M,-)=0, iff Tor_1(M,R/I)=0 for all (f.g.) ideals I; Tor may be computed from flat resolutions in either variable (Flat Resolution Lemma 3.2.8).
Projectivity/injectivity via Ext: Ext^i(A,-)=0 for i>0 when A projective; conversely Ext^1(A,-)=0 forces A projective, Ext^1(-,B)=0 forces B injective.

viewpoints.summary: Algebraic/module-theoretic: Ext and Tor as derived functors of Hom and ⊗ on R-modules, computed by resolutions.
Categorical/derived: Ext as Hom in D(A) to a shift; Tor as homology of the derived tensor product; abelian categories treated like module categories via Freyd-Mitchell.
Homotopical: Dold-Kan turns Hom(P,I) into a simplicial abelian group/space whose homotopy groups are Ext; nLab writes Ext^n as π_0 of maps into B^nA.
Topological: Tor and Ext appear as the correction terms in universal coefficient and Künneth theorems (split, non-naturally).
Geometric: Tor computes intersection multiplicities (Serre), i.e. a derived intersection.
Group-theoretic: H^n(G,A)=Ext^n_{ZG}(Z,A), H_n(G,A)=Tor_n^{ZG}(Z,A); H_1(G,Z)=G^{ab}; H^2 classifies group extensions.
Representation-theoretic: Ext^1 between modules over finite-dimensional/incidence algebras, global dimension, exact structures (relative Ext) used for persistence-module invariants.

conventions.summary: Order of arguments: Weibel and nLab write Ext^1(A,B) for extensions 0→B→X→A→0 ('extension of A by B', quotient first). Stacks writes 'Yoneda extension of B by A' 0→A→...→B→0 with class in Ext^i(B,A) — same pattern. Group-theory texts often say 'extension of N by Q' the other way round (unverified here).
Indexing: Ext^i, R^i with upper (cohomological) indices; Tor_i, L_i with lower (homological) indices; long exact sequences move up resp. down in index.
Sidedness: Tor^R_n(A,B) with A a right and B a left R-module (Weibel, Arapura); Tor^R(M,N) ≅ Tor^{R^op}(N,M), symmetric only for commutative R.
Over Z, many topology sources write Tor(A,B) and Ext(A,B) for Tor_1 and Ext^1 since higher ones vanish.
Derived-category convention allows Ext^i for all integers i (negative ones vanish for objects); shifts written A[n], nLab identifies A[n] with delooping B^nA.
Pontryagin dual A* = Hom(A,Q/Z) (Weibel); commutative-algebra papers use M*=Hom(M,R), Matlis dual M^vee, canonical dual M^dagger.
Terminology slip seen in sources: one REU paper calls Ext the 'left-derived' functor of Hom; standard usage is right derived (Hom is left exact).
conventions.source: Zhukova, 'A Look at the Functors Tor and Ext' (UChicago REU 2018) §6

examples.summary: Tor(Z/m,Z/n) ≅ Z/gcd(m,n) and Ext(Z/m,Z/n) ≅ Z/gcd(m,n); e.g. Tor(Z/4,Z/6)=Z/2.
Ext(Z/n,Z)=Z/n; for finitely generated A, Ext(A,Z) is the torsion subgroup T(A); Ext(Z/p,M)=M/pM.
Base ring matters: Ext^1_Z(Z/2,Z/2)=Z/2 but Ext^1_{Z/2}(Z/2,Z/2)=0.
Resolution of R/x by 0→R→R→R/x→0 for a non-zero-divisor x: Tor_0=M/xM, Tor_1=Ann_M(x), higher vanish; dually for Ext.
examples.source: Hochster-style Tor notes; Wikipedia Tor; Arapura Thm 5.25

examples.summary: Koszul complex: for a polynomial ring over a field, Tor/Ext of the residue field form exterior algebras (Koszul duality).
Flat but not projective: Q over Z; finitely presented flat modules are projective (Weibel Thm 3.2.7).
Extensions of Z/p by Z/p: Weibel Exercise 3.4.1 counts them (p classes in Ext^1, vs only two isomorphism types of middle group Z/p^2 and Z/p⊕Z/p — the latter count from memory).
Ext(A,Z) for torsion A is the Pontryagin dual of A (Weibel Ex. 3.3.3, where p-adic integers appear); lim^1 of a tower of groups is linked to Z_p in Ex. 3.5.5.
Universal coefficient: H^n(C;Z) ≅ (H_n/T_n) ⊕ T_{n-1} for finitely generated homology.

computation.summary: Standard recipe: choose a projective (free) resolution of one variable, apply Hom(-,B) or ⊗B, take (co)homology; over a PID two-term resolutions suffice so only degrees 0,1 occur.
Use additivity: Ext/Tor commute with finite direct sums (Ext turns sums in first variable into products), reducing finitely generated abelian groups to cyclic pieces.
Long exact sequences from short exact sequences in either variable, derived from the snake lemma; used for dimension shifting and comparisons.
Flat resolutions may replace projective ones for Tor; localisation commutes with Tor and (for finitely presented modules over Noetherian rings) with Ext.
Double complex/spectral sequence arguments: combining a free resolution of M and injective resolution of ω_R to get Ext-Tor duality and five-term exact sequences.
Explicit cochain complexes for derived functors of lim over posets (Roos complex), and Mittag-Leffler for vanishing of lim^1.
Koszul complex resolves R/(x_1..x_n) for a regular sequence, giving explicit Tor/Ext.

confusions.summary: 'Ext seems like just diagram chasing; what does higher Ext mean?' Answers: n-extensions (Yoneda), homotopy groups of a mapping space via Dold-Kan, and independence of resolution as the conceptual point.
Inequivalent extensions can have isomorphic middle terms: Ext^1 counts equivalence classes (commuting with the fixed sub and quotient), not isomorphism classes of the middle module.
Splittings in universal coefficient and Künneth sequences exist but are not natural.
Ext depends on the base ring (Ext over Z vs over Z/2 example).
Projective ⇒ flat holds for modules but can fail in non-classical settings (solid modules); Tor needs both variables resolved there.
Yoneda Ext and derived-functor Ext agree when there are enough projectives or injectives; otherwise only Yoneda (or derived-category) Ext is available.
Left vs right derived: Hom is left exact so Ext is a right derived functor; Tor is left derived since ⊗ is right exact. Some expository texts misstate this.
Tor symmetry Tor(M,N)≅Tor(N,M) is not formal: it needs balancing; Arapura notes Rotman's proof is incomplete and points to Weibel Thm 2.7.2.
